Wretched is the mother, and wretched is the one who raises him.'" Ibn Mardawayh also transmitted a similar hadith from Abu Ayyub al-Ansari.

Ibn al-Mubarak also transmitted a similar hadith from Abu Ayyub.

Some say it is Meccan, with no disagreement.

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Surat al-Qari'a was revealed in Makkah."

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Al-Qari'a (the Striking Calamity) is one of the names of the Day of Resurrection, because it strikes hearts with terror and strikes the enemies of Allah with punishment. The Arabs say: "al-qara'athum al-qari'a" (the calamity struck them) when a dreadful matter befalls them.

Ibn Ahmar said:

"And a striking calamity of the days, were it not for their way, would have left you alone for a while."

Another said:

"When we strike them with your manliness, they are struck, and no fire is kindled for us in the cooking pot."

Al-Qari'a is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is His saying: ﴿What is the Striking Calamity?﴾ The majority read it in the nominative case, while 'Isa read it in the accusative, with the implied sense: "Beware the Striking Calamity." The interrogative form serves to magnify and exalt its matter, as its explanation was given earlier in His saying: ﴿The Inevitable Reality﴾ ﴿What is the Inevitable Reality?﴾ ﴿And what will make you know what the Inevitable Reality is?﴾ [al-Haqqa: 1-3]. It is also said that the meaning of the speech is a warning.

Al-Zajjaj said: "The Arabs issue warnings and incitements with the nominative just as with the accusative," and he cited the poet's verse:

"They are worthy of fidelity when the one who is brave in battle says: 'The weapon! The weapon!'"

Taking it in the sense of magnification and exaltation is more preferable, and it is supported by the placing of the noun in place of the pronoun, for it is more indicative of this meaning.

It is also supported by His saying: ﴿And what will make you know what the Striking Calamity is?﴾, for it is an emphasis on the severity of its terror and the extreme dreadfulness of it, to the point that it is as if it lies outside the circle of created knowledge, such that no understanding of any of them can grasp it. Here "ma" (what) in the interrogative is the subject (mubtada'), and "adraka" is its predicate; and "ma al-Qari'a" is a subject and predicate, the whole clause being in the place of the accusative as the second object (maf'ul thani). The meaning is: "What has informed you of the matter of the Striking Calamity?"

Then Glory be to Him explained when the Striking Calamity will occur, saying: ﴿On the Day when mankind will be like scattered moths﴾. The accusative of the time-expression is by an implied verb indicated by "al-Qari'a," i.e., "it will strike them on the Day when mankind will be..." etc. It is permissible that it be accusative by the implied verb "udhkur" (remember).

Ibn 'Atiyya, Makki and Abu al-Baqa' said: it is accusative by "al-Qari'a" itself. It is also said that it is the predicate of an implied subject, the full sense being: "The Striking Calamity will come upon you; the Day when..." Zayd ibn 'Ali read "Yawmu" in the nominative, as the predicate of the implied subject.

Al-Farash (moths) are the birds you see falling into fire and lamps; the singular is farasha. Thus said Abu 'Ubayda and others.

Al-Farra' said: al-Farash is the flying creature among gnats and others, and from it comes the locust. He said: with it is struck the proverb for levity and foolishness: "More hasty than a moth." He recited:

"The moth of forbearance, Pharaoh of torment, and if his generosity is sought, he is a dog, and beneath him is a dog."

And another verse:

"There were peoples whose wisdom was returned upon them, and they were like moths in ignorance."

By "al-mabthuth" is meant the scattered and dispersed. It is said: "baththahu" when he scattered it. A similar statement is His saying, Glory be to Him, in another verse: ﴿As if they were scattered locusts﴾ [al-Qamar: 7]. He said "al-mabthuth" and not "al-mabthutha," because both are permissible, as in His saying: ﴿trunks of uprooted palm trees﴾ [al-Qamar: 20] and ﴿trunks of hollow palm trees﴾ [al-Haqqa: 7]. The explanation of this has already been given.

﴿And the mountains will be like fluffed-up wool﴾, i.e., like wool dyed in various colors that has been carded with a bow. In the language of the scholars, 'ihn' is wool dyed in various colors. This has already been explained in Surat "Sa'ala Sa'il." Descriptions of the mountains on the Day of Resurrection have been mentioned in the Mighty Book, and we have already presented the reconciliation between them.

Then Glory be to Him mentioned the states of people and their division into two groups in summary, saying: ﴿As for he whose scales are heavy﴾ ﴿he will be in a pleasant life﴾. The discussion of the balance has already been presented in Surat al-A'raf, Surat al-Kahf and Surat al-Anbiya'.

Here it has been differed over: it is said that "mawazin" is the plural of "mawzun," meaning the deed that has weight and worth before Allah, and this is the view of al-Farra' and others. It is also said that it is the plural of "mizan," the instrument in which the records of deeds are placed, and it is expressed in the plural form, just as one says "for every event there is a mizan." It is also said that by "mawazin" are meant the proofs and evidences, as in the verse of the poet:

"Indeed I had before your meeting a single argument, for every adversary a mizan of his own."

The meaning of "'ishatin radiyatin" is: a pleasing life that its possessor is pleased with.

Al-Zajjaj said: that is, one of contentment which its possessor is content with. It is also said "'ishatin radiyatin" means "pleasing" (fa'ila lil-rida), namely, one that brings contentment, which is gentleness and submission to its people.

"Al-'Isha" is a word that comprises the blessings that are in Paradise.

﴿And as for he whose scales are light﴾, i.e., whose bad deeds outweigh his good deeds, or who has no good deeds of account. ﴿His mother will be the Abyss﴾, i.e., his dwelling place is Hell. He called it his mother because he takes refuge in it as one takes refuge in his mother. "Al-Hawiya" is one of the names of Hell, and it was named "hawiya" because he falls (yahwi) into it, given the depth of its bottom. From this is the saying of Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt:

"The earth is our refuge, and it was our mother; in it are our graves, and in it we are born."

And the saying of another:

"O 'Amr, if our spears should reach you, you would be like one whom the Abyss (al-Hawiya) has hurled."

"Al-mahwa" and "al-mahwah" mean the space between two mountains. "Tahawa al-qawm fi al-mahwa" means when some of the people fell one after another.

Qatada said: the meaning of "fa-ummuhu hawiya" is: his destination is the Fire.

'Ikrima said: because he falls into it upon the top of his head.

Al-Akhfash said: "ummuhu" is "mustaqirra" (settled, abiding).

﴿And what will make you know what it is?﴾ This interrogative is for terrifying and dreadful effect, indicating that it is outside what is known, such that human knowledge cannot encompass it and one cannot know its reality.

Then Glory be to Him explained it, saying: ﴿A blazing Fire﴾, i.e., its heat has reached its extreme and has attained the utmost intensity. "Nar" is in the nominative as the predicate of an implied subject: i.e., "it is a blazing Fire."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted through several chains from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "al-Qari'a is one of the names of the Day of Resurrection."

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from him regarding His saying ﴿His mother will be the Abyss﴾ that he said: "like the saying 'his mother has fallen (hawat ummuhu).'"

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from 'Ikrima regarding ﴿His mother will be the Abyss﴾ that he said: "the top of his head is the Abyss in Hell."

What did such-and-such a woman do?' If he has died and has not come to them, they say: 'He has been taken off to his mother, the Abyss (al-Hawiya). Wretched is the mother, and wretched is the one who raises him.'" Ibn Mardawayh also transmitted a similar hadith from Abu Ayyub al-Ansari.
